statement: Whether khipu (Andean knotted-string devices) constitute writing at all, beyond a purely numerical/accounting notation, is itself a live dispute distinct from any origin-type question. Gary Urton (Signs of the Inka Khipu: Binary Coding in the Andean Knotted-String Records, University of Texas Press, 2003) argues khipu construction (fiber, ply direction, knot type/direction, attachment) encodes binary-coded information beyond pure accounting, explicitly against a "mere mnemonic" reading. Newly analyzed epistolary khipu with as many as 95 distinct symbols (within logosyllabic range, well beyond pure-accounting khipu's symbol count) and statistical studies reporting Zipf/Shannon-entropy signatures consistent with natural-language structure (matching Quechua entropy figures) have been presented as evidence of intelligible content, but these remain indirect statistical arguments, not confirmed readings. Colonial Spanish sources describe khipu used for histories, genealogies, poetry, and law, but no confirmed decipherment of narrative content exists. Mainstream caution holds most khipu are confidently readable only as numerical/accounting records.
scholarly_disagreement: Urton and subsequent statistical work argue for narrative/linguistic content beyond accounting; mainstream caution holds only numerical content is confidently read — actively debated, not resolved.
